findings.entity: symptoms/* (all 22 symptom pages; template site/entity.js urgentHtml)
findings.explanation: Template-level gap in red-flag signposting. The symptom template prints each page's `urgent` list under the heading 'Seek urgent care if' with no routing line, and the data supply none: content/symptoms.json contains no '999', '112', 'NHS 111', 'A&E' or 'ambulance' on any of the 22 pages. Only chest-pain, numbness and weakness say 'call emergency services' (first bullet only). back-pain, abdominal-pain, pelvic-pain, vaginal-bleeding, rash, knee-pain and joint-pain call something 'an emergency' without saying whom to call. 'Urgent care' is ambiguous in UK usage (urgent treatment centre, GP, NHS 111, A&E), and the lists mix true 999 situations (thunderclap headache, non-blanching rash with fever, blue lips or breathlessness at rest, saddle numbness with bladder or bowel change, swelling of the tongue or face, collapse in possible pregnancy, thoughts of self-harm) with 'GP appointment within days' items (breast-lump[0], heavy-periods[4], vaginal-bleeding[2]) in one undifferentiated box, so a reader cannot tell which is which. conditions.json already tiers its advice (999/A&E vs NHS 111 vs GP, e.g. ectopic-pregnancy, lung-cancer, deep-vein-thrombosis); symptoms do not, and first-aid emergency topics show a 999/112/911 callout that symptom pages lack. The site footer says only 'call your local emergency number'; NHS 111 is never named on a symptom page.
findings.suggestedFix: Add one standard routing line to the urgent block and tier each bullet in the data (for example 999/A&E; same-day NHS 111 or GP; GP appointment soon), taking the wording from the NHS pages already cited on each page. Minimum: name 999 (or 112) on the life-threatening bullets (headache, shortness-of-breath, rash, back-pain cauda equina, abdominal/pelvic pain in possible pregnancy, fever with non-blanching rash) and move the GP-appointment items out from under 'urgent care'.

findings.quote: Central chest pain or pressure, like a tight band or heavy weight, lasting more than 15 minutes
findings.explanation: The page tells the reader to call emergency services immediately (steps[0]) and not to let the person 'see if it passes' (dont[0]), yet the recognition criterion and callFor[0] ('Chest pain or discomfort lasting more than 15 minutes, or shorter but with breathlessness, sweating, collapse or a known heart condition') make a 15-minute duration part of what counts as a heart attack. symptoms/chest-pain says 'lasting more than a few minutes ... call emergency services'. A reader using 'Recognise it' as the trigger can reasonably wait up to 15 minutes, and the two pages in this set disagree. First aid for a suspected heart attack should not be gated on duration.
findings.suggestedFix: Drop the fixed duration from recognise[0] and callFor[0] (for example 'chest pain or pressure that does not ease with rest: call 999 straight away, do not wait to see if it passes') and use the same wording on symptoms/chest-pain; if a time is kept, make it identical on both pages.

findings.quote: Heat exhaustion: headache, dizziness and confusion, nausea and loss of appetite, heavy sweating, pale clammy skin, cramps in the arms, legs and stomach, fast weakening pulse and rapid breathing, temperature 38-40°C, thirst, weakness
findings.explanation: Confusion is listed as a sign of heat exhaustion, but the same page says that in heat exhaustion 'the person is still thinking clearly' (summary and recognise[2]), tells the reader to treat new confusion as heatstroke and call emergency services (steps[3]; callFor[0] 'Any confusion, unusual behaviour, seizure ...') and says 'Do not wait to see if a confused person improves' (dont[3]). A confused casualty could be filed under the less urgent heat-exhaustion list. The wording was possibly copied from a source list that names confusion under both conditions.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove 'and confusion' from the heat-exhaustion list (keep 'dizziness') and add that any confusion, change in behaviour or fit means heatstroke: call 999.

findings.quote: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes, or one seizure after another without recovery
findings.explanation: The summary says a seizure over 5 minutes 'is a medical emergency', but the page never tells the reader to call 999/112: no step says it, the callFor list sits under the generic 'Get medical help when' heading, and because the topic is emergency:false the page shows no 999/112/911 callout (the hub facet even labels it 'Not usually an emergency'). The only 'ambulance' wording is in the 'Afterwards' step, which says someone with known epilepsy who recovers fully does not usually need one.
findings.suggestedFix: Start the callFor list with 'Call 999 (or 112) if' and add a step along the lines of 'note the time; call 999 if it lasts 5 minutes, is a first seizure, repeats, or there is injury or breathing difficulty'.

findings.quote: Signs of infection, or a tetanus vaccination more than 10 years ago (5 for dirty wounds)
findings.explanation: The 10-year booster rule (5 years for dirty wounds) is US practice presented as general on a UK-first site. In the UK, five doses of tetanus-containing vaccine (infancy, pre-school, teenage) are regarded as giving long-term protection and there is no routine 10-yearly booster; wound management depends on whether the course is complete, unknown or incomplete and on how tetanus-prone the wound is (UKHSA Green Book tetanus chapter; NHS tetanus pages). As written, fully vaccinated UK adults are told they may need care, while someone with an incomplete course who was vaccinated recently is implicitly reassured. The cited NHS cuts-and-grazes and bites pages are not a plausible source for this rule.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with UK wording, for example 'signs of infection, or a tetanus vaccination history that is unknown or incomplete (in the UK five doses give long-term protection), especially with a deep, dirty or contaminated wound or a bite', and cite the NHS tetanus/vaccination page or UKHSA Green Book. If no UK source is added, remove the 10/5-year figures.

findings.quote: Thoughts of self-harm alongside exhaustion and low mood
findings.explanation: A self-harm red flag sits in the 'Seek urgent care if' list with no route to help: no 999 for immediate danger and no GP, NHS 111 or crisis-line signposting (for example Samaritans 116 123). This is the one symptom bullet where the specific service matters most to a UK reader.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a line such as 'If you are in immediate danger call 999; otherwise contact your GP, NHS 111 (mental health option where offered) or Samaritans on 116 123 (free, 24 hours)', after checking current numbers against the NHS and Samaritans pages.

findings.quote: Burns with breathing difficulty, soot around the nose or mouth, or from an enclosed fire
findings.explanation: The topic is emergency:false, so the page shows only the 'Get medical help when' list, and none of its four items (all chemical and electrical burns; burns larger than the hand, deep, or on face, hands, feet, genitals or joints; inhalation signs; young children, older people, pregnancy, shock) says where to go or whom to call. The words 999, 112, 111, A&E and ambulance appear nowhere on the page. UK advice sends these burns to A&E, and breathing difficulty, large or deep burns and shock to 999. The same pattern, to a lesser degree, is on wound-care ('spurting blood') and sprains ('Seek urgent care if').
findings.suggestedFix: Head the list 'Go to A&E, or call 999 if ...' and separate the 999 items (breathing difficulty or smoke inhalation, large or deep burns, signs of shock) from the A&E ones; add 'call NHS 111 if unsure'.

findings.quote: otherwise call the poisons information line or emergency services for advice
findings.explanation: Generic wording that fits countries with a public poison-centre line (US, Ireland) but not the UK: the UK National Poisons Information Service serves healthcare professionals (TOXBASE), and members of the public are directed to NHS 111, A&E or 999. A UK reader has no 'poisons information line' to call, and NHS 111 is never named on the page.
findings.suggestedFix: Name the UK route: 'otherwise call NHS 111 (UK), or your local poison centre elsewhere; call 999/112 if in any doubt'.

findings.quote: Disabling fatigue over six months, worsened by exertion, diagnosed after excluding other causes.
findings.explanation: 'Over six months' is the older duration used by US/IOM-era criteria. NICE NG206 (2021), the UK guideline, says to suspect ME/CFS after about 6 weeks in adults (4 weeks in children) and to confirm the diagnosis once symptoms have lasted about 3 months; post-exertional malaise is a core feature. A reader could wait far too long. Neither cited page (NHS tiredness and fatigue; NHS iron-deficiency anaemia) covers ME/CFS.
findings.suggestedFix: Say 'persistent disabling fatigue that is worse after exertion, lasting weeks to months; diagnosed by a clinician after other causes are considered' (drop the six-month figure) and add NICE NG206 or the NHS ME/CFS page as a reference.

findings.explanation: Tingling from ulnar nerve entrapment (the page's own commonCauses[1]) involves the ulnar nerve, not a vein; a vein is not a source of paraesthesia. The neighbouring tags (flexor retinaculum, cervical disc) are nerve-compression sites, so this looks like a mis-mapped structure name (ulnar nerve to ulnar vein).
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with the ulnar nerve structure, or remove the tag.

findings.explanation: The title is generic ('Broken bone') but the URL (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/broken-arm-or-wrist/) is the NHS page for a broken arm or wrist. The first-aid page covers thigh, hip, pelvis, spine, open fractures and dislocations, which that page does not.
findings.suggestedFix: Retitle as 'NHS: Broken arm or wrist' and add a reference that covers leg, hip, pelvis and spine injuries and dislocations.

findings.quote: Fever in a baby under three months (38 °C or more) or under six months (39 °C or more)
findings.explanation: These infant thresholds match NICE NG143 (fever in under 5s) but are not plausibly supported by the two cited pages (NHS fever in adults; NHS sepsis). The same list's 'fever lasting more than five days' is a child-fever cut-off on a page whose main NHS reference is the adult page.
findings.suggestedFix: Add NICE NG143 and the NHS fever-in-children page as references, or soften to 'any fever in a young baby'.

findings.quote: Mild ankle swelling that clears overnight.
findings.explanation: Pregnancy is offered only as a benign cause ('Prolonged standing, heat and pregnancy'). There is no red flag for swelling in pregnancy: sudden or severe swelling of the face, hands or feet, especially with headache, visual disturbance or pain under the ribs, can signal pre-eclampsia and needs same-day maternity assessment. The urgent list's face/lip/tongue bullet is framed as allergy, not this. (headache.urgent does carry a pregnancy flag.)
findings.suggestedFix: Add an urgent bullet for sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet in pregnancy, especially with headache or visual changes: contact the midwife or maternity unit the same day, or 999 if severe; cite the NHS pre-eclampsia page.

findings.quote: when these happen on most days (NICE uses more than about 12 times a month)
findings.explanation: 'Most days' (more than about 15 days a month) is stricter than the NICE wording given in the brackets, which is symptoms on a persistent or frequent basis, particularly more than 12 times a month. The plain-language gloss and the NICE figure disagree, and a reader with symptoms on 13 days a month would not meet 'most days'. The bullet's action is a GP visit although it sits under 'urgent'.
findings.suggestedFix: Write 'frequently or persistently (NICE: more than about 12 times a month)' and drop 'on most days'.

findings.quote: Bleeding after sex on more than one occasion, or bleeding between periods that continues for more than a few cycles
findings.explanation: symptoms/heavy-periods urgent[4] says 'Bleeding between periods, after sex or after the menopause, which needs a GP appointment even when it is light' with no repeat-episode threshold, while this page sets 'more than one occasion' and 'more than a few cycles' (and calls post-menopausal bleeding an 'urgent GP appointment' where heavy-periods says only 'a GP appointment'). Two pages in the same set give different thresholds for the same symptom, and a reader could take 'more than one occasion' to mean a single episode of bleeding after sex can be ignored.
findings.suggestedFix: Use one wording on both pages (for example 'bleeding after sex or between periods that is unexplained or recurs: see a GP') and keep 'urgent GP appointment' for post-menopausal bleeding.

findings.quote: Neurons exhaust their energy stores within minutes, ending most seizures; beyond 5 minutes the mechanisms that stop them are failing (status epilepticus) and brain injury becomes likely without drugs that boost GABA inhibition, such as midazolam.
findings.explanation: Seizures end through active inhibitory and ionic mechanisms, not because neurons run out of energy, and the sentence then says the stopping mechanisms 'fail', which contradicts it. Five minutes is the practical threshold after which a convulsion is unlikely to stop unaided and treatment is started; neuronal injury becomes likely after much longer continuous seizure activity, not at 5 minutes.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword: 'Most seizures stop by themselves within a couple of minutes as the brain's own inhibitory systems take over; one that continues beyond 5 minutes is unlikely to stop unaided (status epilepticus), and prolonged seizures can injure the brain, so emergency treatment such as midazolam is given.'

findings.quote: One 300 mg tablet chewed slowly (or 4 x 75 mg).
findings.explanation: UK first-aid and NHS/BHF advice specifies a single 300 mg aspirin tablet, chewed; the '4 x 75 mg' alternative is not part of that advice, and low-dose 75 mg tablets are often gastro-resistant (slow to absorb), so they are not equivalent for this purpose. It also adds a count-and-chew decision for a bystander under stress.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove '(or 4 x 75 mg)'; keep 'one 300 mg aspirin, chewed slowly, if available and not allergic', as in the cited NHS and BHF pages.

findings.quote: Morning stiffness lasting over an hour in a young adult, better with exercise.
findings.explanation: Descriptions of inflammatory back pain / axial spondyloarthritis usually cite morning stiffness of about 30 minutes or more (with onset in a young adult, improvement with exercise but not rest, and night pain); 'over an hour' is closer to the rheumatoid arthritis convention and would exclude people who fit the pattern. I am not certain which threshold the cited NICE/NHS pages use.
findings.suggestedFix: Say 'prolonged morning stiffness (30 minutes or more)' or remove the figure.

notes: 18 findings (1 high, 7 medium, 10 low); nothing was dropped for the 20 cap. 'cleanEntities' means no entity-specific finding: every symptom page is still covered by finding 1 (template-level signposting). CPR and choking (pending re-check, 2021 edition): read against Resuscitation Council UK 2021 and St John Ambulance practice and found no clear error in the steps, so none are reported. Not reported because arguable rather than clearly wrong: cpr.why calls ventricular fibrillation 'the commonest rhythm at collapse' (true for witnessed cardiac collapse, but asystole/PEA are commoner across all out-of-hospital arrests); choking step 4 calls emergency services only after the first back-blow/thrust cycle fails while the page callout says call at once. The generic first-aid disclaimer in site/entity.js ('Written to follow current resuscitation and first-aid guidance') sits oddly beside the pending-recheck notice on those two pages. Signposting: the fixes are mostly schema/template work (a tier per urgent bullet plus a standard 999 / A&E / NHS 111 line); conditions.json seekCare already models the tiered style, and symptoms.json and first-aid.json contain no 'NHS 111' or 'A&E' at all. Emergency:true first-aid topics (heart-attack, choking, severe-bleeding, poisoning, allergic-reactions, hypothermia, cpr, stroke, heatstroke, electric-shock) get the 999/112/911 callout; emergency:false topics (burns, fractures, sprains, fainting, seizures, wound-care) do not, and only fractures and fainting name a service in their steps. Symptom pages describe rather than diagnose; closest to diagnostic wording is swelling.what ('usually means fluid retention from the heart, kidneys, liver or medications', which omits the venous causes listed lower down). Unverified offline and left out of the findings: the burns reference URL path '/calendar/first-aid/' (British Burn Association) looks like an events path; the pelvic-pain citation to NICE CG122 'Detection in primary care' may have been superseded by the ovarian cancer recommendations in NG12; the shortness-of-breath '92% on a home oximeter' threshold is not in the cited NHS or Asthma + Lung UK pages and UK oximetry advice varies (<=92% vs <92%); the breast-lump 'GP appointment within days rather than weeks' timing is unsourced.
